**Total internal reflection and the critical angle**
When light travels from a medium with a higher refractive index to one with a lower index and hits the boundary at more than the critical angle, it is completely reflected instead of refracted. The critical angle equals the arcsine of n2 over n1. This effect traps light inside optical fibers and waveguides.

**Law of reflection (angle of incidence equals angle of reflection)**
The basic law of reflection: the angle between the incoming ray and the surface normal equals the angle between the reflected ray and the normal. Both rays lie in the same plane as the normal. This holds exactly for specular reflection from smooth surfaces such as mirrors.

**Brewster's angle**
The angle of incidence at which p-polarized light (polarized in the plane of incidence) is not reflected at all. At this angle the reflected and refracted rays are perpendicular, so unpolarized light that reflects there comes out fully linearly polarized. Its tangent equals n2 over n1 (Brewster's law).

**Specular vs. diffuse reflection**
Specular reflection happens at smooth surfaces and produces a clear mirror image, since all rays obey the law of reflection together. Diffuse reflection happens at rough surfaces, where light scatters in many directions, which is why paper looks matte.

**Lambert's cosine law (Lambertian reflectance)**
Describes an ideal diffuse surface whose radiant intensity varies with the cosine of the angle from the surface normal. Such a surface looks equally bright from every viewing direction (isotropic). The Oren–Nayar model extends diffuse reflection to rougher surfaces.

**Fresnel equations**
Equations giving the reflection and transmission coefficients for s- and p-polarized light at a boundary between two media. At normal incidence the reflectance is ((n1 − n2)/(n1 + n2)) squared. By conservation of energy, reflectance and transmittance add up to one.

**Frustrated total internal reflection and evanescent waves**
During total internal reflection, an evanescent wave reaches a short distance past the boundary and fades rapidly. If a second medium is brought very close, some of that energy tunnels across, "frustrating" the reflection. This is an optical analog of quantum tunneling and is also the basis of TIRF (total internal reflection fluorescence) microscopy.

**Phong reflection model**
A computer graphics shading model developed by Bui Tuong Phong. It combines ambient, diffuse, and specular reflection terms weighted by the constants ka, kd, and ks. James Blinn modified it into the Blinn–Phong model.

**Schlick's approximation**
A simple formula, widely used in computer graphics, that approximates the Fresnel reflection coefficient as a function of the angle of incidence.

**Reflection coefficient in transmission lines (capital gamma)**
In electrical signal lines, reflection happens whenever a signal meets an impedance mismatch. The reflection coefficient Γ equals (Z_load − Z_0)/(Z_load + Z_0), and its magnitude relates to the standing wave ratio as (SWR − 1)/(SWR + 1). It is often plotted on a Smith chart, and the Bergeron diagram method also analyzes these reflections.

**Hagen–Rubens relation**
Relates the reflectivity of a metal to its electrical conductivity at low (infrared) frequencies. Higher conductivity means higher reflectivity, which is why metals make good mirrors.

**Spectralon**
A fluoropolymer material made to be an almost perfect Lambertian (diffuse) reflector. It is used as a reflectance standard in spectrophotometry and for instrument calibration.

**Anti-reflective thin films (quarter-wave coatings)**
Coatings that cancel reflection through destructive interference. The ideal film is a quarter-wavelength thick and has a refractive index equal to the square root of the substrate's index (when used in air). They are used on camera lenses and eyeglasses.

**180-degree phase shift on reflection**
When light reflects off a medium with a higher refractive index, its phase flips by 180 degrees (a polarity inversion). Reflection off a lower-index medium causes no flip. This matters for thin-film interference.

**Retroreflection and reflecting telescopes**
Retroreflectors, such as cat's-eye reflectors and the BLITS satellite, send light straight back toward its source. Reflecting telescopes like Isaac Newton's Newtonian design use mirrors instead of lenses, and catoptric systems form images using reflection alone.
